closest_works.citation: MIST-RL: Mutation-based Incremental Suite Testing via Reinforcement Learning (arXiv:2603.01409)
closest_works.what_it_does: RL-trains a test generator with an 'incremental mutation reward' (reward only when a new test kills a mutant that survived all prior tests), producing compact high-mutation-score suites on HumanEval+/MBPP+. Then it USES those suites to rerank code candidates: a consensus matrix V_ij tracks which candidates pass which suites, Score(c_i) = sum_j V_ij. Reports reranking accuracy 48.78% on HumanEval+ vs 45.73% for CodeRM-8B, i.e. +3.05 pts, explicitly framed as 'mutation-derived suites are superior verifiers'.
closest_works.how_it_differs: The mutation signal is consumed entirely at suite-CONSTRUCTION time and then thrown away: at selection time every verdict is one equal, non-negative vote, with no per-test weight, no likelihood ratio, and no per-cluster localization. This is the single most dangerous paper for KAPPA -- not because it does KAPPA's mechanism, but because it already banks KAPPA's headline motivation ('mutation information improves downstream code selection'). KAPPA can no longer claim that idea; it can only claim the mechanism (signed per-verdict LLR indexed by cluster). It also silently creates a mandatory new baseline: mutation-hardened suite + uniform vote. If that baseline matches KAPPA, F4 fires and the LLR machinery is decorative.

closest_works.citation: B4: Towards Optimal Assessment of Plausible Code Solutions with Plausible Tests (arXiv:2409.08692, ASE 2024)
closest_works.what_it_does: Bayesian posterior over (which solutions correct, which tests correct) given the pass matrix. Eq. 3 defines P(E_ij=1 | X_i=0, Y_j=1) = theta_1 (incorrect solution passes a CORRECT test) and P(E_ij=1 | X_i=0, Y_j=0) = theta_0. Eq. 8 puts Beta priors on theta_0, theta_1, theta_x, theta_y (eight hyperparameters); Eq. 9 gives a conjugate closed form scoring consensus sets with four Beta functions. Hyperparameters set as theta_0 ~ (alpha=1, beta>>1), theta_1 ~ uniform (alpha_1 = beta_1 = 1).
closest_works.how_it_differs: theta_1 is EXACTLY the quantity KAPPA calls 1 - kappa_lj, and B4 confirms it is (i) a single scalar shared by every test and every candidate, (ii) given a flat uninformative prior and marginalized, never estimated from executable evidence, and (iii) verified not to vary per cluster. KAPPA's claimed delta vs B4 is therefore real and unusually crisp: KAPPA supplies an executable estimator for B4's theta_1, indexed by (test j, cluster l). This is the strongest and most defensible framing available -- 'B4 with a measured theta_1' -- and it is stronger than the vaguer 'measures instead of priming' phrasing in the proposal. Risk: a reviewer will ask why you do not simply do Empirical-Bayes on B4 (fit theta_1 from the pass matrix), which is a cheaper competitor KAPPA must beat.

closest_works.citation: EvoOtter: Evolutionary Reproduction Test Generator (arXiv:2607.02854)
closest_works.what_it_does: Evolutionary generation of bug-reproduction tests where the fitness/selection operator IS the mutation kill rate: mutants are generated, each candidate test is scored by how many it kills, high-kill tests are retained into the next generation. Ablates three selection strategies -- mutation-score, LLM-based, random -- on TDD-Bench-Verified and SWE-Rebench, and finds mutation-based selection best (random slightly beats LLM-based when combined with crossover).
closest_works.how_it_differs: This is the closest anyone gets to 'kill rate as a selection criterion', and it answers half the kill question: yes, kill rate is used for SELECTION, but it selects TESTS, not code candidates. The kill rate is a hard top-half filter (a binary retain/discard), not a signed weight on an individual verdict; it is global per test, computed against mutants of one reference program, and never conditioned on which candidate cluster is being judged. Useful for KAPPA as evidence that kill rate carries real selection signal, and as a warning: EvoOtter's own ablation shows random selection nearly matches an LLM-based selector, which is exactly the kind of 'machinery is decorative' result F4 is designed to catch.

closest_works.citation: ACES: Who Tests the Tests? Leave-One-Out AUC Consistency for Code Generation (arXiv:2604.03922)
closest_works.what_it_does: w_j = max(0, (LOO-AUC_j(w_unif) - 1/2) * p_j(1-p_j)) for ACES-C; ACES-O optimizes max_w sum_j w_j(LOO-AUC_j(w) - 1/2) on the simplex. Weights are computed per-problem from that problem's pass matrix. Baselines: Majority Voting, CodeT, MBR-exec, SC+Spec, Self-collaborate, MPSC, DS^3.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Confirms gaps (a) and (b) as stated: the max(0, .) clip means no weight is ever negative, tests with LOO-AUC <= 1/2 get exactly zero, and the reference ranking is the tally-induced one. Verified: the paper contains NO discussion of mutation testing or kill rates anywhere in its related work. But one correction to the proposal's framing -- ACES weights are per-problem, not pooled, so the 'no per-problem reliability estimation' gap (c) is wrong as written for ACES; the correct statement is 'no per-CLUSTER (within-problem) reliability'. More dangerous: ACES Fig. 3 already partitions by mean discriminative power and reports that in the Hard region (delta-bar <= 0) 'no method passes more than 1 of 14 tasks'. The decisive stratum is therefore already documented, already known to defeat every existing method, and -- critically -- appears to contain on the order of 14 tasks. F2 as drafted has almost no statistical power.

closest_works.citation: Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression: A Measurement Study of Post-Hoc Falsification Operators for Frozen Small Code Models (arXiv:2606.16999)
closest_works.what_it_does: Measures 26 semantic output-space operators (execution consensus/MBR-Exec, embedding medoid, behavioral trace ranking, learned verifiers, fingerprint correctness prediction, version-space elimination, metamorphic veto, counterexample-guided repair, adaptive sampling). Uses a deterministic probe bank of <=24 inputs (public-test args plus type-aware INPUT mutations) to build execution fingerprints. Central negative result: no operator over the semantic output space beats Best-of-N at matched compute, explained by a 'coverage wall', 'capability scissors' (no discriminable error among competent candidates), and a 'near-empty consensus trap'.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Not a mutation-weighting method (its mutations perturb INPUTS to build fingerprints, not programs to estimate specificity), so it does not scoop KAPPA's mechanism. It is instead the most serious attack on KAPPA's PREMISE: it argues empirically that the stratum where post-hoc selection could help is close to empty at matched compute. KAPPA must distinguish its regime (this study is frozen SMALL models with visible public tests; ACES/B4 assume no public tests and larger models) and must pre-register the measured size of the decisive stratum before claiming F2 is winnable. Ignoring this paper would be the fastest route to a desk reject.

closest_works.citation: Code Generation by Differential Test Time Scaling / DiffCodeGen (arXiv:2605.20473)
closest_works.what_it_does: Coverage-guided fuzzing synthesizes inputs with NO existing tests and NO LLM calls; all candidates are executed on those inputs; candidates are clustered by behavioral similarity; the medoid of the largest cluster is returned. Competitive with or superior to SOTA test-time scaling at a fraction of the time and tokens.
closest_works.how_it_differs: No mutants, no per-test weights -- it is pure behavioral clustering plus the tally. Two consequences for KAPPA. First, KAPPA's Step 1 (cluster by behavioral fingerprint on test inputs) is fully established prior art (also CodeT consensus sets, SRank, AlphaCode clustering) and must not be presented as contribution. Second, it is the sharpest F5 threat: it achieves near-SOTA at essentially zero marginal cost, so KAPPA's L*K*M extra executions (for L=10, K=20, M=100 that is ~20k executions per problem) must be justified against 'largest-cluster medoid for free' plus 'spend the same budget on more candidates'. NOTE: an automated summarizer initially told me this paper compared against CodeT, B4 and ACES; I checked the verbatim abstract and that was fabricated. Do not cite it as a baseline comparison.

closest_works.citation: DiffTGen (Xin & Reiss, ISSTA 2017) and the mutation-based patch-correctness line (Shibboleth, ISSTA 2022; Invalidator, arXiv:2301.01113; PATCH-SIM, arXiv:1706.09120; Ghanbari's patch-validation/mutation-testing duality, arXiv:1912.00117)
closest_works.what_it_does: DiffTGen builds a 'target program' from the syntactic difference between buggy and patched code, generates test inputs that expose semantic differences between the two, and classifies a patch as overfitting if a distinguishing test reveals wrong output. The broader line assesses patch correctness by perturbing/comparing candidate patches and measuring their impact on production and test code, ranking correct patches top-1 in 43% of cases; Ghanbari explicitly frames patch validation and mutation testing as dual problems.
closest_works.how_it_differs: This is the deepest and least-cited-by-the-proposal ancestor of KAPPA's central assumption: using syntactic variants of a CANDIDATE program as proxies for nearby wrong programs is a decade-old idea in APR, not new. What the APR line never does is convert the variant-kill statistics into a probability -- variants are used to GENERATE a discriminating test or to CLASSIFY one patch, never to assign a signed likelihood ratio to each verdict in an N x M matrix. KAPPA must cite this line explicitly or a software-engineering reviewer will consider the novelty claim uninformed.

closest_works.citation: Mutation-driven LLM test-generation line: MuTAP (arXiv:2308.16557), Meta ACH (arXiv:2501.12862, FSE 2025), MutGen (arXiv:2506.02954), PRIMG (arXiv:2505.05584), Test vs Mutant (arXiv:2602.08146), STING (arXiv:2604.01518), SWE-Mutation (arXiv:2605.22175)
closest_works.what_it_does: All feed surviving mutants back into prompts or search to build stronger suites or harder benchmarks. MuTAP reaches 93.57% mutation score by re-prompting on each surviving mutant; ACH generated 9,095 mutants and 571 hardening tests across 10,795 Kotlin classes at Meta; PRIMG prioritizes surviving mutants by a subsumption-graph model; STING uses surviving variants of the ground-truth patch to diagnose under-constrained SWE-bench suites (77% of instances admit a surviving variant, augmentation drops resolve rates 4.2-9.0%); SWE-Mutation scores suites by Relative Detection Rate.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Verified across all seven: mutants are used to BUILD suites or to GRADE benchmarks, and in every case the mutation signal terminates before any candidate-selection step. None weights a verdict, none produces a likelihood ratio, none conditions on a candidate cluster. KAPPA's claimed delta vs the mutation-testing line survives contact with this literature intact -- this is the cleanest of KAPPA's three claimed deltas.

closest_works.citation: Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults? (Just et al., FSE 2014) vs Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? (Papadakis et al., ICSE 2018) and the ASE 2020 revisit
closest_works.what_it_does: Just et al. established mutant-fault coupling and is the standard citation for mutants-as-proxy. Papadakis et al. re-ran the question on CoreBench and Defects4J and found that ALL correlations between mutation score and real fault detection become weak once test suite size is controlled for, concluding the reported correlations were largely a confounding artifact of suite size.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Not a selection method -- this is the evidence base that decides whether KAPPA's central assumption is even admissible, and it is more hostile than the proposal assumes. F1 as drafted (raw corr(kappa_lj, true P(fail|incorrect)) > 0.5) is precisely the kind of unconditioned correlation Papadakis showed to be confounded. In KAPPA's setting the suite-size confound maps onto test j's global strictness/pass rate p_j: a strict test kills more mutants AND fails more incorrect programs, so raw correlation will look good for reasons that carry no localization information. F1 must be restated as a PARTIAL correlation controlling for p_j, and must be evaluated separately within wrong clusters, since that is the only stratum where kappa_lj has to work.

prior_art.what_is_genuinely_new:
ANSWER TO THE KILL QUESTION: No. I could not locate any work that converts mutant kill rates into per-verdict weights or likelihood ratios for candidate SELECTION. The kill-rate-to-selection link exists only for selecting or evolving TESTS (EvoOtter's kill-rate fitness, PRIMG's subsumption prioritization, MIST-RL's incremental mutation reward). Every located mutation paper terminates its mutation signal before the candidate-ranking step, and every located candidate-ranking paper (CodeT, MBR-exec, SRank, B4, ACES, S*, DiffCodeGen, MPSC, Coder-Reviewer, LEVER) reaches selection with no mutation signal at all. Three things survive as genuinely unclaimed:

1. WITHIN-PROBLEM, PER-CLUSTER LOCALIZATION OF TEST RELIABILITY. This is the strongest and cleanest novelty. Every mutation-testing result in the field computes ONE kill rate per test against mutants of ONE reference program. Letting kappa_lj vary with the cluster l being judged -- so a test can be "tight around the wrong cluster and vacuous around the right one" -- has no located precedent in either literature. B4 was verified to hold theta_1 constant across all clusters; ACES weights are per-problem but constant across candidates within a problem.

2. SIGNED PER-VERDICT EVIDENCE. Confirmed: ACES clips at max(0, .), CodeT/MIST-RL/DiffCodeGen count uniform non-negative votes, B4 marginalizes rather than weights. LLR(fail) = log(eps_j / kappa_lj) going negative -- a failure that is evidence FOR a candidate because the test is known to be indiscriminate locally -- is unclaimed.

3. AN EXECUTABLE ESTIMATOR FOR B4's theta_1. Frame KAPPA this way; it is the most defensible positioning available and it is exact, since 1 - kappa_lj is literally B4's P(pass | incorrect) with (j, l) indices attached.

WHAT IS NOT NEW, AND MUST BE DROPPED FROM THE CLAIMS: Step 1 behavioral-fingerprint clustering (CodeT/SRank/DiffCodeGen). The idea that mutation information improves downstream code selection -- MIST-RL published this with a +3.05 pt reranking number. Using syntactic variants of a candidate as proxies for nearby wrong programs -- DiffTGen and the APR patch-correctness line have done this since 2017. Claimed gap (c) as written is factually wrong: ACES does estimate per-problem, not pooled; restate it as per-cluster.

THE SHARPEST TECHNICAL ATTACK ON THE CENTRAL ASSUMPTION (not covered by the drafted falsifiers): the ESTIMAND SILENTLY CHANGES MEANING ACROSS CLUSTERS. When r_l is correct, its AST mutants are wrong programs and kappa_lj is a genuine estimate of P(fail | incorrect). When r_l is wrong, its mutants are DIFFERENTLY-wrong programs, essentially none of which is the correct program, so kappa_lj estimates "how well test j separates r_l from its own syntactic neighborhood" -- a different quantity. The LLRs are therefore not on a common scale, yet score_l = sum_j LLR_lj compares them directly across clusters. This is a correctness bug in the scoring rule, not merely a validity concern, and it is exactly where the decisive stratum lives. Second attack: equivalent mutants. AST-level operators produce them at nontrivial rates (Meta's ACH needed a dedicated detector, precision 0.79 / recall 0.47), they deflate kappa_lj, and since LLR(fail) = log(eps_j / kappa_lj) diverges as kappa_lj approaches 0, the clipping in step 4 is load-bearing in a way that hides the bias rather than controlling it.

IMPROVED FALSIFIERS:
F1' (replaces F1): PARTIAL correlation of kappa_lj with true P(fail | incorrect), controlling for test j's global pass rate p_j, because Papadakis et al. ICSE 2018 showed raw mutation-score/fault-detection correlations collapse once the size/strictness confound is removed. Require it separately within WRONG clusters, the only stratum that matters. Threshold on the partial, not the raw, correlation.
F1b (new): measure the equivalent-mutant rate per cluster and report kappa_lj sensitivity to it; show results with and without an equivalent-mutant filter. If the clip in step 4 is doing the work, the estimator is not identified.
F2' (replaces F2): pre-register the MEASURED SIZE of the decisive stratum and a power analysis before running it. ACES Fig. 3's Hard region is on the order of 14 tasks and no method exceeds 1 of 14 there; a win on that stratum is not distinguishable from noise. Either use a benchmark where the stratum is large enough or state the minimum detectable effect.
F4' (replaces F4): the drafted trivial baselines are too weak. Add (i) MIST-RL-style mutation-hardened suite with UNIFORM votes -- this isolates whether the LLR machinery adds anything over merely having mutation-aware tests, and it is the baseline most likely to kill KAPPA; (ii) DiffCodeGen largest-cluster medoid, which is free; (iii) Empirical-Bayes B4, i.e. B4 with theta_1 fit from the pass matrix instead of a flat prior, which is the cheap competitor a reviewer will demand.
F5' (extends F5): DiffCodeGen achieves near-SOTA with zero LLM calls and no tests, so the matched-budget arm must include "spend L*K*M executions on additional candidates" (Best-of-N), which arXiv:2606.16999 reports beats all 26 post-hoc operators it measured.
F6 (new): CROSS-CLUSTER CALIBRATION. Test directly whether LLR scores are comparable across clusters when some r_l are correct and some are wrong. If scores are systematically inflated for wrong clusters, the summation is invalid and the method's decisive-stratum claim is unsupported regardless of F1.
F7 (new): SIGNED-WEIGHT ABLATION. Run KAPPA with LLRs clipped at zero (ACES-style). If performance is unchanged, then claim (2) -- negative per-verdict weight, the headline differentiator -- is decorative even if the overall method wins.
prior_art.search_confidence:
Moderate-to-high on the kill question, with two explicit caveats.

Coverage: ~20 targeted searches plus direct reads of ACES (2604.03922), B4 (both the abstract and a successful ar5iv extraction of the Bayesian model with Eq. 3/8/9 and hyperparameter settings), MIST-RL, EvoOtter, SWE-Mutation, DiffCodeGen (verbatim abstract), the falsification-operators measurement study, symbolic equivalence partitioning, and the Test-vs-Mutant adversarial paper. I probed the kill question from at least seven independent phrasings (kill-rate weighting, likelihood ratio per verdict, downweighting tests with surviving mutants, mutation-based verifier for best-of-N, per-problem test false-negative estimation, mutants as proxies for incorrect programs, mutation at inference time) and the result set converged on the same cluster of suite-improvement papers, which is the signature of genuine absence rather than of a bad query. I also deliberately crossed into the APR patch-correctness literature and the SBFL/Barinel Bayesian-diagnosis literature, since both formalize P(test outcome | component faulty) and are the most likely places for an unnoticed scoop; Barinel's intermittent-failure health parameter is structurally the same object as KAPPA's theta, applied to fault localization rather than candidate selection, and is worth a citation as an adjacent formalism.

Caveat 1 -- reliability of automated summaries. One WebFetch summary of DiffCodeGen fabricated a baseline comparison against CodeT, B4 and ACES; I caught it by pulling the verbatim abstract, and the real paper compares none of them. Treat every claim above that I did not verify against primary text with corresponding suspicion. The B4 model details, the ACES formula and Fig. 3 hard-region numbers, the MIST-RL uniform-vote scoring rule, and the DiffCodeGen abstract were all verified against primary sources.

Caveat 2 -- date horizon. Many of the most relevant items (ACES 2604.03922, MIST-RL 2603.01409, EvoOtter 2607.02854, the falsification study 2606.16999, DiffCodeGen 2605.20473, STING 2604.01518) postdate my training and are known to me only through search results and fetches, so I cannot cross-check them against background knowledge. Given the density of 2026 activity in exactly this area -- test-quality-aware selection on one side, mutation-guided test generation on the other -- the two halves KAPPA joins are converging fast, and a preprint doing per-cluster kill-rate weighting could appear in the next few months. Before committing, I would run a direct arXiv full-text and Semantic Scholar citation-graph search on the forward citations of B4, ACES and MuTAP, which I could not do through this search interface.

Confidence that no published work does per-cluster kill-rate-to-signed-LLR for candidate selection: high. Confidence that KAPPA's overall contribution is large rather than incremental: low -- MIST-RL owns the motivating result and B4 owns the probabilistic frame, so KAPPA is the conjunction of two published halves, which is why I graded CLOSE_PRIOR_ART rather than ADJACENT_ONLY.

closest_works.citation: B4: Towards Optimal Assessment of Plausible Code Solutions with Plausible Tests (arXiv:2409.08692) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.08692
closest_works.what_it_does: Bayesian selection over the pass matrix. Defines four latent parameters: theta_x = P(solution correct), theta_y = P(test correct), theta_1 = P(incorrect solution passes a CORRECT test), theta_0 = P(incorrect solution passes an INCORRECT test). Places Beta conjugate priors on all four, marginalizes them out analytically, and scores each consensus set (i.e. behavioral cluster) by a posterior that is a product of four Beta functions B(n1+1, |E1|-n1+1)·B(n0+1, |E0|-n0+beta_0)·B(nx+alpha_xy, N-nx+1)·B(ny+alpha_xy, M-ny+1). Selects the consensus set maximizing this posterior; formalized as an integer program with a tractable approximation whose error is bounded by prior correctness.
closest_works.how_it_differs: This is the real threat and it dismantles three of the four claimed deltas. (1) theta_1 IS the specificity term 1 - P(fail|incorrect) that KAPPA claims to be the first to address, and it is NOT merely 'primed via a Beta prior' — it is marginalized against observed counts n1, so B4 already estimates it from the pass matrix, per problem, in closed form. The honest delta is localization (per test x per cluster), not estimation-vs-assumption. Restate the claim or a reviewer will kill it. (2) B4's likelihood already makes a test's evidential contribution depend on which candidate set is hypothesized correct — only passing events from incorrect solutions in the hypothesized set enter n0/n1 — so 'weight varies within-problem across candidates' is already present, in a principled joint form. KAPPA's difference is that the reliability PARAMETER is indexed by cluster (kappa_lj) rather than shared (theta_1). (3) A Bayesian posterior over pass/fail events is intrinsically signed per verdict: a pass against a probably-correct test is positive evidence, a fail is negative. So gap claim (a), 'no located work assigns NEGATIVE weight to a test verdict,' is false as written — it is only true for the narrow class of linear per-test weight vectors (CodeT, ACES, VeRPO). What genuinely survives: B4 uses ONE global theta_1 shared across all tests and all clusters, has no mechanism to say 'test j is tight around cluster l but vacuous around cluster l-prime,' generates no mutants, and has no per-test reliability at all.

closest_works.citation: ACES: Who Tests the Tests? Leave-One-Out AUC Consistency for Code Generation (arXiv:2604.03922) — https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03922v1
closest_works.what_it_does: Weights tests by consistency with the tally-induced ranking: w_j = max(0, LOO-AUC_j(w_unif) - 1/2) · p_j(1-p_j) (ACES-C), plus ACES-O which iteratively optimizes a differentiable LOO-AUC objective on a majority-vote-prefiltered top-K shortlist. Assumption 4 requires only that the AVERAGE discriminative power be positive: delta_bar > 2·sqrt(ln2/m).
closest_works.how_it_differs: Verified directly against the paper text. Confirmed: weights are clipped at zero so no test can be negative; weights are per-problem but UNIFORM across all candidates within a problem (a single w_j applies to every candidate); no candidate clustering; the Related Work (Sec. 5, citing CodeT, MBR-exec, SRank, ALGO, S*, Coder-Reviewer, LEVER, MPSC, DS3, CURE, CoCoEvo, Self-debugging, ConVerTest, TestCase-Eval) contains no mutation testing, no per-cluster weighting, no abstention, and no discussion of the tally-cluster-wrong failure mode. Correction to your framing: Assumption 4 is a per-problem average over the m tests of THAT problem, not a cross-problem pooled reliability estimate — 'ACES Assumption 4 = pooled' is a mischaracterization you should fix, since ACES is already per-problem; what it lacks is per-CLUSTER, which is your actual delta. Your gap (b), that LOO-AUC inverts on the tally-wrong stratum and zeroes exactly the rescuing tests, is a genuine and unaddressed mechanical criticism — I found no paper making it. That is your strongest unclaimed argument; lead with it, not with 'no negative weights.'

closest_works.citation: MIST-RL: Mutation-based Incremental Suite Testing via Reinforcement Learning (arXiv:2603.01409) — https://arxiv.org/html/2603.01409
closest_works.what_it_does: Trains a test generator with RL where reward is granted only when a new test kills a mutant that survived all previous tests (marginal-utility / incremental kill reward). Explicitly motivates this by downstream code reranking: reports mutation score as the best quantifier of a suite's discriminative power and ~3.05% reranking accuracy gain over strong baselines via a consensus reranking protocol on an N x K pass matrix.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Establishes the mutation-score -> test-discriminativeness -> better-reranking causal chain that KAPPA relies on, which removes much of the surprise from your mechanism. But three separations hold and you should state them precisely: (i) mutants are injected into the REFERENCE solution, which requires ground truth — KAPPA mutates cluster representatives with no labels, which is the actually hard part; (ii) mutation operates at test-GENERATION/training time, not at inference over a fixed suite; (iii) reranking is plain uniform vote summation over the pass matrix — no per-test weight, no per-cluster localization. Note the flip side: MIST-RL is a budget-competitive rival to KAPPA. If mutation-derived signal is best spent generating better tests up front rather than discounting verdicts after the fact, KAPPA loses on F5. Add MIST-RL-style mutation-guided test generation at matched execution budget as a falsifier baseline; F4's 'trivial baselines' do not cover it.

closest_works.citation: Dawid & Skene (1979), Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Observer Error-Rates Using the EM Algorithm; and Snorkel-style programmatic weak supervision label models
closest_works.what_it_does: Latent-truth aggregation over noisy voters. Per-voter confusion matrices estimated by EM; the label model converts per-source accuracies to log-odds weights w_j = log(alpha_j/(1-alpha_j)) and sums signed votes, with an explicit abstain symbol. Weights are negative whenever alpha_j < 1/2 (anti-correlated source).
closest_works.how_it_differs: KAPPA's step 4 IS this machinery. LLR(pass) = log((1-eps_j)/(1-kappa_lj)) and LLR(fail) = log(eps_j/kappa_lj) is the standard class-conditional log-odds of a two-sided-error noisy voter; scoring by sum_j LLR_lj is the standard label-model score. Signed and per-verdict weights are textbook here, not novel — which independently refutes gap claim (a) in its general form. ACES itself cites Dawid & Skene. The novelty is confined to the ESTIMATOR for the incorrect arm: getting kappa_lj without labels, localized to a cluster, from AST mutants. Frame the paper that way (a new estimator plugged into a known aggregator) rather than as a new aggregation scheme, or the contribution will read as smaller than it is once a reviewer recognizes the formula.

closest_works.citation: Welinder, Branson, Belongie, Perona, The Multidimensional Wisdom of Crowds (NeurIPS 2010); GLAD (Whitehill et al. 2009); MACE
closest_works.what_it_does: Models annotator competence as multidimensional and item-dependent rather than a single scalar: infers annotator competence, bias, and item difficulty jointly, explicitly representing groups of annotators whose skill varies by region of the item space (items easy for annotators preferring one attribute, hard for those preferring another).
closest_works.how_it_differs: This is the conceptual ancestor of per-(test, cluster) reliability: 'voter reliability localized to a region of item space' is a solved and named problem in crowdsourcing, roughly 16 years old. KAPPA transplants it to (test, behavioral-cluster) pairs in code selection, which is a legitimate first for this domain, but you cannot claim the statistical idea. The transplant is nontrivial in one respect worth emphasizing: crowdsourcing infers region-specific competence from redundant labels via EM, whereas KAPPA MANUFACTURES the local negative class with mutants — that is the actual novelty and it is exactly the thing F1 must defend.

closest_works.citation: Just, Jalali, Inozemtseva, Ernst, Holmes, Fraser, Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing? (FSE 2014); Papadakis et al., Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? (ICSE 2018)
closest_works.what_it_does: Empirically tests the mutant-real-fault coupling hypothesis on 357 real faults. Finds a statistically significant correlation between mutant detection and real fault detection independent of coverage, but also that many real faults are coupled to NO mutant under standard operators, and (ICSE 2018) that the observed correlation is largely explained by the confound of test suite size/strength.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Not prior art on the method — prior art on your CENTRAL ASSUMPTION and it substantially pre-empts F1. F1 as drafted (corr(kappa_lj, true P(fail|incorrect)) > 0.5) will almost certainly PASS for a reason that is worthless to you: a test that kills many mutants is simply a stronger/broader assertion, so it also fails many wrong programs, generating correlation with zero localization content. That confound is precisely what F4's per-test global pass-rate baseline captures, so a passing F1 plus a passing F4-baseline means the machinery is decorative. Fix F1 to be a PARTIAL correlation, controlling for (a) test j's global fail rate against all wrong candidates in the problem and (b) mutant-kill rate averaged over all clusters — i.e. test whether the CLUSTER-SPECIFIC residual of kappa_lj predicts the cluster-specific residual of P(fail|incorrect at cluster l). Only the within-problem, within-test, across-cluster variance component is your claim. Report it as a variance decomposition, not a raw correlation.

closest_works.what_it_does: Empirically characterizes the distribution of real LLM code errors. closest_works.how_it_differs: Direct empirical evidence against KAPPA's central assumption, and it predicts the failure DIRECTION. Single-token AST mutants (comparison flips, off-by-one, branch deletion, return perturbation) are killed by almost any test that exercises the mutated line, whereas the actual nearby wrong programs fail only on corner cases and whole-algorithm misreads. So kappa_lj will be systematically INFLATED for broad, generic, high-coverage tests and will under-separate the rare corner-case test — which is exactly the test that rescues the decisive stratum. That means the misspecification is not zero-mean noise; it is biased against F2, the falsifier you most need to pass. Two concrete mitigations worth pre-registering: (i) draw the local negative class from OTHER CLUSTERS' representatives (a real, LLM-generated, semantically distinct wrong program at distance) in addition to AST mutants, and ablate mutants-only vs. cross-cluster-only vs. both — if cross-cluster-only wins, the AST-mutant apparatus is dead weight and you have a cleaner, cheaper paper; (ii) add coarse-grained mutants (loop-bound rewrites, whole-branch substitution, algorithm-level swaps) and pre-register that fine-grained-only underperforms. Also note the clustering finding cuts against you structurally: if LLM errors are highly clustered, wrong candidates concentrate in a FEW large clusters, so the tally-top-wrong stratum is both common (good for F2's importance) and hard (the wrong cluster is large and internally consistent, so its mutants are unrepresentative of the correct cluster's neighborhood).

prior_art.what_is_genuinely_new: Not located anywhere: a per-(test, cluster) reliability parameter for code-candidate selection, estimated at INFERENCE time, from label-free AST mutants of behavioral-cluster representatives, and plugged into a signed per-verdict log-likelihood-ratio score that never references the tally or any induced ranking. Each ingredient exists separately — signed log-odds aggregation (Dawid-Skene / weak supervision), the specificity parameter theta_1 (B4), per-test weighting from the pass matrix (ACES, VeRPO), behavioral clustering (CodeT, SRank, Semantic Voting, SEP), mutation-derived test discriminativeness feeding reranking (MIST-RL), region-dependent voter competence (Welinder et al.), abstention with clustering (ESE) — but the composition, and specifically the localization of the incorrect-arm likelihood to a cluster, is unpublished. Two smaller genuine firsts: (i) the conflict-graph toxicity guard inflating eps_j for mutually unsatisfiable tests — ImpossibleBench (arXiv:2510.20270) constructs contradictory test suites to measure reward hacking but nobody uses satisfiability conflict structure to discount verdicts at selection time; (ii) the mechanical argument that ACES's LOO-AUC reference ranking inverts on the tally-wrong stratum and therefore zeroes precisely the rescuing tests — I found no paper stating this, and it is a sharper, more defensible framing than 'nobody uses negative weights.' THREE CLAIMED DELTAS MUST BE WITHDRAWN OR REWRITTEN. (1) 'No located work assigns negative weight to a test verdict' is false: B4's Bayesian likelihood is signed per verdict by construction, and weak-supervision label models use w = log(alpha/(1-alpha)) which is negative for alpha < 1/2. It is true only for the narrow family of clipped linear per-test weight vectors. (2) 'vs B4 — measures the specificity term instead of priming it via Beta prior' is unfair: B4 marginalizes theta_1 against observed counts n_1, so it estimates it from data; the real delta is that theta_1 is one scalar shared across all tests and clusters whereas kappa_lj is indexed by both. (3) 'weight varies within-problem across clusters' is partially anticipated: B4's likelihood already makes each test's evidential contribution depend on the hypothesized correct-solution set. Also, 'ACES has no per-problem reliability, only pooled (Assumption 4)' is a misreading — ACES weights are already per-problem; Assumption 4 is a within-problem average over that problem's m tests. The surviving, defensible one-line claim is: reliability localized to (test x behavioral cluster), estimated without labels or a reference ranking. FALSIFIER REPAIRS, in priority order. F1 is the weakest link and will pass for the wrong reason — a raw corr(kappa_lj, P(fail|incorrect)) > 0.5 is nearly guaranteed by the pure test-strength confound (broad assertions kill mutants AND fail wrong programs), which is exactly the signal F4's global pass-rate baseline already captures. Replace it with a variance decomposition: does the cluster-specific RESIDUAL of kappa_lj (after removing test-j main effect and cluster-l main effect) predict the cluster-specific residual of true P(fail | incorrect near l)? Pre-register a threshold on that residual correlation, not the raw one; the mutant-real-fault literature (Just FSE 2014, Papadakis ICSE 2018, which found the mutation-score/fault-detection correlation largely dissolves once suite strength is controlled) tells you the raw version is uninformative. F2 is missing three baselines that attack the same stratum at similar cost: SEP (symbolic equivalence partitioning, arXiv:2604.06485), MIST-RL-style mutation-guided test GENERATION at matched budget, and B4 itself (which is a stronger comparator than CodeT and is currently absent from ACES's own table). F4 needs an inverse-difficulty / p(1-p) weighting arm — VeRPO shows difficulty weights alone are worth up to +8.83 pass@1 in the RL setting and ACES already embeds p_j(1-p_j), so difficulty is the cheapest confound that could mimic your gains, and uniform + global-pass-rate do not cover it. F3's 0.5-point no-harm band is too loose to be a real constraint given typical HumanEval+ variance at N=50; tighten or specify seeds and a paired test. F5 is correct to exist but understates the problem: L·K·M at L=10, K=20, M=20 is 4,000 extra executions per problem against a 1,000-cell base pass matrix, a 5x blowup, and 5x more candidates is a famously strong baseline — state the ratio in the abstract rather than the appendix, and report a kappa-estimation ablation at K=5 so the budget claim has somewhere to retreat to. Finally, add a pre-registered ablation that could kill the AST-mutant apparatus outright and would make a cleaner paper if it wins: estimate the local negative class from OTHER CLUSTERS' representatives (real, LLM-generated, semantically distinct wrong programs, already executed, marginal cost zero) instead of from synthetic mutants. Given the finding that LLM errors are multi-line, semantic, corner-case-omission-dominated (54.4% on HumanEval+) and highly clustered — nothing like single-token AST perturbations — cross-cluster negatives are plausibly the better proxy AND free, which would eliminate the entire K-mutant execution cost and the whole of F5.

prior_art.what_is_genuinely_new:
SURVIVES: the estimator itself. I found no work that mutates *cluster representatives of the candidate pool* at inference, with no labels and no reference solution, and plugs the resulting per-(cluster,test) kill rate into a per-verdict score. The novel unit is the SECOND INDEX on kappa_lj. Nothing located estimates a test-reliability quantity that varies across candidates *within* a problem. That is the whole defensible contribution — it should be the paper's title claim.

DOES NOT SURVIVE — three of the four claimed deltas are wrong as stated:

1. Gap (a) "no located work assigns NEGATIVE weight to a test verdict" is FALSE twice over. B4's log-posterior already contains signed per-verdict contributions (a fail against theta_1/theta_0 contributes negative log-mass), and ARBITER (2605.26172) explicitly accumulates *signed additive log-ratio evidence with per-source reliability factors r_f, r_g in [0,1]* — structurally the same object as sum_j LLR_lj — on exactly the wrong-majority stratum. It is math, not code, which is your escape hatch, but the architecture is published. Narrow the claim to: "no method in the linear-weighted-tally family (CodeT / MBR-exec / ACES) admits signed per-verdict weights."

2. Delta vs B4 is much narrower than claimed. B4 ALREADY has (i) behavioral clustering — its consensus sets group solutions by identical pass patterns, so "cluster candidates by behavioral fingerprint" is not new; (ii) a specificity parameter — theta_0 = P(pass | incorrect solution) is exactly your 1-kappa; (iii) per-problem (not pooled) estimation. Your real delta is two-fold and should be stated precisely: B4 *integrates theta_0 out* under Beta(1, beta_0>>1), yielding a score that is a product of Beta functions over sufficient-statistic COUNTS — exchangeable, non-additive; KAPPA *plugs in* a per-cluster point estimate, yielding an additive naive-Bayes LLR. And B4's theta_0 is one number per problem; yours is one per (cluster,test). KAPPA is best framed as "B4 with a localized, empirically-grounded theta_0" — that is a legitimate paper, but it is an estimator swap inside B4's scaffold, not a new framework.

3. Gap (c) "no per-problem reliability estimation" is FALSE for B4 (its posterior is computed per problem). It is TRUE for ACES (Assumption 4 is global). Restate as per-CLUSTER, not per-problem.

CONFIRMED AND STRONG — gap (b) is your best asset. I verified against v1 and v2 (12 Jul 2026): ACES computes LOO-AUC_j against the ranking induced by w_unif, then clips with max(0, . - 1/2). When the uniform tally is anti-correlated with truth, a rescuing test necessarily scores below 1/2 and is zeroed. ACES v2 Sec 4.3 *observes* the failure (delta-bar<=0 "Hard region", no method passes more than 1 of 14 MBPP tasks, "the pass matrix alone is insufficient") but misattributes it to low average test quality rather than to reference-ranking inversion, and proposes static analysis as the remedy. That mechanistic diagnosis is unpublished and is worth a paper section on its own.

BUT THE FALSIFIERS HAVE A HOLE THAT INVALIDATES F2: ACES v2 reports ACES-O beats ACES-C precisely when delta-bar<=0 (16/52 vs 9/52). ACES-O drops the uniform reference ranking and optimizes iteratively — i.e. ACES ALREADY SHIPS a partial fix for your decisive stratum. F2 names only ACES-C, the variant you have shown is structurally broken there. Beating it is a strawman result. F2 must target ACES-O or it is not a test.

FOUR TECHNICAL ATTACKS ON THE MECHANISM:

(i) FATAL-IF-UNADDRESSED — kappa saturates on FAIL verdicts, killing the localization exactly where it matters. If representative r_l fails test j, essentially every AST mutant of r_l also fails j (single-edit mutations almost never *repair* behavior), so kappa_lj -> 1 and LLR(fail) = log(eps_j / kappa_lj) -> log(eps_j). The cluster index vanishes. All within-problem variation lives on PASS verdicts, while FAIL verdicts — the dominant discriminative signal in code selection — collapse to a per-test constant. Your headline claim "weight varies within-problem across clusters" is therefore true only on the less informative half of the matrix. Pre-register a diagnostic: report Var_l(kappa_lj) separately for verdicts where r_l passes vs fails. If the fail-side variance is ~0, the mechanism is doing far less than advertised.

(ii) eps_j is unspecified and is doing most of the work. Given (i), LLR(fail) ~ log(eps_j), so the false-alarm rate governs the decisive verdicts — yet the proposal never says how eps_j is estimated, only that the toxicity guard "inflates" it. This is the single largest under-specification. Mutants cannot estimate eps_j (that needs P(fail | CORRECT), and you have no labeled correct program). Either derive eps_j from the conflict graph explicitly, or admit KAPPA inherits B4's Beta-prior treatment for it — in which case the "measures instead of priming" delta applies to only one of the two parameters.

(iii) Equivalent mutants systematically deflate kappa, and non-uniformly. A well-known 10-30% of mutants are semantically equivalent to the parent (GEM-LLM reports 25-30% of *surviving* mutants are equivalent). These are not "nearby wrong programs" — they are the same program, so they can never be killed, and they drag kappa_lj down hardest on tests with weak oracles, biasing specificity in precisely the direction that makes weak tests look weaker and strong tests look weaker too. Condition F1 on a measured equivalent-mutant rate, or use a trivial-detector filter.

(iv) The central assumption faces a distributional mismatch the mutation literature already documents. AST mutants are single-edit local perturbations; LLM-wrong programs are typically wrong at the spec-interpretation level — a whole coherent basin ("confidently wrong reading of the problem"), which no single-edit mutant of a representative reaches. Papadakis et al. (ICSE 2018) found mutation-score/real-fault correlations become WEAK once test-suite size is controlled; Just et al. (FSE 2014)'s 0.73 was uncontrolled. Your defense — and you should state it explicitly — is that F1 correlates at the PER-TEST level, so the suite-size confound does not apply to you. That is a real and defensible distinction, but it must be argued, not assumed.

FALSIFIER REPAIRS:
F1: good as designed and correctly per-test (immune to the suite-size confound). Add: stratify by whether r_l is correct vs incorrect — the proxy may hold around correct representatives and fail around wrong ones, which is the case you actually need. Add equivalent-mutant rate as a covariate.
F2: swap ACES-C -> ACES-O (mandatory), add B4 with tuned beta_0, and report % of ORACLE HEADROOM RECOVERED within the stratum (ARBITER's denominator), not raw accuracy. Raw accuracy on this stratum is unpowered: ARBITER measured wrong-majority at only 1.8-3.9% of GSM8K at K=24; ACES's hard region is ~14/427 MBPP. On HumanEval+ you will have ~15-25 problems — no power for a binary comparison. Pool MBPP+ and LiveCodeBench across >=3 generator models, pre-register paired McNemar with a stated minimum detectable effect.
F3: 0.5 pts is not the binding risk. ARBITER found that most direct correction strategies DEGRADE a strong consensus baseline and only *conservative additive* evidence helps. Pre-register a margin gate (override the tally only when the LLR margin exceeds tau) and report recoveries/degradations as a signed override ledger.
F4: add two harder trivial baselines — "largest behavioral partition" (SEP-style) and B4-with-tuned-beta_0. Uniform majority alone is too weak to be the decorative-machinery test.
F5: state M. At ACES's M~500 with L=10, K=20, the L*K*M term is ~100k extra executions/problem — comparable to the ENTIRE N*M matrix, so KAPPA roughly doubles cost and cannot claim ACES-like negligible overhead. The strongest matched-budget baseline is spending it on MORE TESTS, which helps CodeT substantially; budget it there, not on more candidates.

BIGGEST THREAT TO THE PREMISE, not the mechanism: 2606.16999 (Jun 2026) formalizes your decisive stratum as the "consensus trap", proves (Lemma 1) that leakage-free selectors can ONLY net-gain there, tests 26 post-hoc operators, and finds ZERO net recovery on every cell — arguing the regime requires generator-verifier weight co-evolution to escape. If that generalizes, KAPPA cannot work by construction. Your rebuttal is real and should be in the paper: their pool is k=8 on 0.5-1.5B models, where a correct candidate is usually absent (they measure trap headroom = 0 for DeepSeek-1.3B). KAPPA assumes N=50 with a competent generator, where headroom demonstrably exists. Measure and report the trap rate and oracle headroom at YOUR N and model scale as a precondition experiment — before any selection results. If headroom is near-zero at N=50 too, stop.

closest_works.citation: Cai, Kulik, Choudhury (Univ. Melbourne) — ARBITER: Reasoning Trajectory Basins and Majority Vote Failures in Test-Time Sampling, arXiv:2605.26172v1 (25 May 2026)
closest_works.what_it_does: Targets 'wrong-majority failures' — correct answer present but outvoted. Groups samples into basins by normalized answer, then accumulates SIGNED additive log-ratio evidence: Delta_2(q) = log((b_2+a)/(b_1+a)) + r_f*log((f_2+a)/(f_1+a)) + r_g*log((g_2+a)/(g_1+a)), where r_f, r_g in [0,1] are reliability factors that downweight a source when its outputs fragment. GSM8K/MMLU-HS-Math/MATH-500; Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4; K=24. Wrong-majority rates 1.8-3.9%. Recovers ~22% of oracle headroom (e.g. Llama: 20 recoveries / 9 degradations = +11 net), no net-negative cell.
closest_works.how_it_differs: This is the paper that falsifies gap (a). It already publishes the exact architecture KAPPA proposes — clustering, then a SIGNED additive log-ratio score with per-source reliability discounting, evaluated on the wrong-majority stratum — and shows it works. KAPPA's escape is domain and evidence source: ARBITER is math-only (explicitly scopes out non-math as future work), groups by final answer not execution fingerprint, and derives evidence from extra LLM calls (framed re-solves, guided re-solves, panel trials) rather than from label-free AST mutants and test verdicts. KAPPA's 'no LLM calls' property is a real efficiency delta against it. Two findings to import: report % of oracle headroom recovered rather than raw accuracy (the only adequately powered statistic at 2-4% stratum size), and heed that broad self-review, hidden-state reranking, and direct basin-selection all DEGRADED the consensus baseline — only conservative additive evidence helped, which argues for a margin-gated override in F3.

closest_works.citation: MIST-RL: Mutation-based Incremental Suite Testing via Reinforcement Learning, arXiv:2603.01409 (Mar 2026)
closest_works.what_it_does: Trains a test-generation policy with GRPO, rewarding tests that kill mutants surviving all previously generated tests (marginal-utility reward alpha*R_qual + beta*Delta, with redundancy penalty). Mutation engine applies six operator categories to the CANONICAL solution. Achieves SOTA mutation score with ~19.3% smaller suites; the resulting suites improve downstream code reranking accuracy on HumanEval+ by 3.05% over CodeRM-8B tests.
closest_works.how_it_differs: The nearest 'mutation meets code reranking' work, and the one a reviewer will cite first — but it lands on the opposite side of every axis KAPPA cares about. Mutation happens at TRAINING time to build a suite, not at inference to discount verdicts; it mutates a GROUND-TRUTH canonical solution, which KAPPA cannot assume; and its actual reranking rule is plain uniform voting, Score(c_i) = sum_j V_ij, with no per-test weights at all. So it improves the pass matrix's INPUTS while KAPPA reweights its OUTPUTS. The proposal's stated delta versus the mutation-testing line holds cleanly here; cite MIST-RL rather than STING (2604.01518) as the primary contrast, since STING augments SWE-bench regression suites from ground-truth patches and is further from selection.

closest_works.citation: Papadakis, Shin et al. — Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? (ICSE 2018); and Just et al. — Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing? (FSE 2014)
closest_works.what_it_does: Just et al. (357 real faults, 5 projects) report 0.73 correlation between mutant detection and real-fault detection, claimed independent of code coverage. Papadakis et al. (Defects4J, CoreBench) re-examine at scale and find ALL mutation-score / real-fault correlations become weak once test-suite size is controlled; the strong uncontrolled correlations are largely a test-suite-size confound.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Directly governs whether F1 can pass, and the two papers disagree — F1's 0.5 threshold sits between them, so cite both and justify the cut. Crucially, the Papadakis critique does NOT straightforwardly apply to KAPPA: the suite-size confound arises when correlating suite-level mutation score with suite-level fault detection, whereas F1 correlates a PER-TEST kappa_lj with a per-test true P(fail|incorrect), where there is no suite size to confound. Make that argument explicitly — it is KAPPA's best defense of the central assumption. The surviving worry is distributional, not statistical: AST mutants are single-edit local faults, while LLM-wrong programs are typically wrong at the spec-interpretation level (a coherent wrong basin), which no single-edit mutant of a representative can reach. Add equivalent mutants as a measured covariate (GEM-LLM reports 25-30% of surviving mutants are equivalent); they can never be killed, deflate kappa_lj systematically, and bias hardest on exactly the weak-oracle tests.

closest_works.citation: Cho, Wang, Sui, Grama (Purdue / Texas Instruments) — Inference-Time Code Selection via Symbolic Equivalence Partitioning, arXiv:2604.06485v2 (11 May 2026)
closest_works.what_it_does: Bounded symbolic execution partitions candidates by functional behavior: each candidate is compared against existing partition representatives, and if no distinguishing input is found within budget it joins that partition. Selects the representative of the largest partition. Public examples used only as a pre-filter. HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench (438 filtered); baselines CodeT, SRank, CodeBLEU/embedding consensus, LLM-as-judge.
closest_works.how_it_differs: Establishes that inference-time behavioral partitioning with representative selection is already standard, further eroding the novelty of KAPPA's steps 1-2 (together with B4's consensus sets). What it conspicuously lacks is everything KAPPA adds: no per-test reliability, no weighting of any kind (pure largest-partition, uniform), no mutation, no signed scores. It also concedes the decisive stratum without addressing it, reporting problematic partition structures on 505/8,969 consensus-eligible instances (5.63%) as a limitation. Useful two ways: as an independent estimate that the decisive stratum is ~5-6%, which constrains F2's power budget; and as the 'largest behavioral partition' baseline that F4 should add, since it is a far stronger trivial baseline than uniform majority.

closest_works.citation: He, Wang, Wang, Ouyang, Chen — Code Generation by Differential Test Time Scaling (DIFFCODEGEN), arXiv:2605.20473 (May 2026); and CoVerRL: Breaking the Consensus Trap in Label-Free RL, ACL 2026
closest_works.what_it_does: DIFFCODEGEN obtains inputs via coverage-guided fuzzing on one candidate, executes all candidates on those inputs, clusters by dynamic behavior, and picks the candidate with shortest relative distance to others in the largest cluster — no additional LLM inference. CoVerRL names the same 'consensus trap' failure (self-consistency training collapses diversity and reinforces systematic errors) and escapes it by alternating generator and verifier roles so the two co-evolve, gaining 4.7-5.9% on math with self-verification rising from ~55% to >85%.
closest_works.how_it_differs: DIFFCODEGEN is a third independent instance of behavioral-clustering-plus-largest-cluster selection at inference (confirming that part of KAPPA is well-trodden), but applies uniform cluster-size scoring with no per-test weighting and no mutation; treat my characterization as the least verified item here, as two sources conflicted on whether it weights tests. CoVerRL matters as the source of the claim 2606.16999 leans on — that escaping the consensus trap requires WEIGHT updates. KAPPA is a frozen-weight method, so it is implicitly betting against both. Worth one paragraph of positioning: KAPPA's wager is that execution-grounded mutant evidence is a qualitatively different signal from the self-consistency signal that CoVerRL shows collapses, because mutants are generated mechanically and cannot inherit the generator's spec misreading.

refutations.verdict:
FATAL. On the single realistic task I built (HumanEval-98-style `count_upper`, 1 correct + 8 conceptually-wrong candidates, 18 tests, real AST mutants), KAPPA selects a WRONG program (W_allpos, tally 12) while plain uniform-weight majority selects the CORRECT one (tally 16). KAPPA ranks the correct program 3rd. This is robust to deleting the two deliberately-broken tests, and it persists when eps_j is supplied by an ORACLE with hidden labels — so eps estimation is not the bottleneck; the scoring rule itself is.

The diagnosis is an exact algebraic identity, verified to 1.4e-14:
    score_l = SUM_j log(eps_j/kappa_lj) + SUM_{j:PASS} [ logit(kappa_lj) + logit(1-eps_j) ]
Three consequences kill the design as specified:

(1) KAPPA is a monotone-amplified majority vote. Every passed test contributes a strictly POSITIVE amount whenever kappa_lj > eps_j. The mechanism cannot invert a verdict, only re-gain it — so on the decisive stratum (F2) it cannot "rescue" a candidate by reweighting; it can only re-rank when fragility differences overwhelm tally differences. Empirically score ~ 3.77*tally + const, R^2 = 0.59: the tally that "never enters" explains most of the score.

(2) The gain term logit(kappa_lj) rewards MUTANT FRAGILITY, which is a syntactic property orthogonal to correctness. Controlling for the pass row, +0.10 in mean kappa buys +10.27 nats = 3.03 free passing tests. And corr(mean kappa, is_correct) = -0.142 — fragility is if anything anti-correlated with correctness. The terse wrong program W_allpos wins precisely because it is terse (5 mutation sites, all lethal, kappa saturating at 1.00).

(3) Sufficiency violation, demonstrated on real code: `correct` and `W_perword` have IDENTICAL pass rows (111111011111111011, tally 16 each). The pass matrix is the only behavioral evidence available, so they are evidentially indistinguishable — yet KAPPA separates them by 1.42 nats and ranks the WRONG one higher, purely on mutant fragility.

Two further independent failures: the flagship novelty (a) "negative weight to a test verdict" requires kappa_lj < eps_j, which occurs in 0/162 cells at any eps <= 0.10 — the novelty never fires at plausible eps, and when it does fire it is produced entirely by the eps prior, not by the mutant machinery. And F1 is not a falsifier: a mutant-free null (fraction of candidates failing test j, zero extra executions) scores corr = 0.998 / 1.000 against true P(fail|incorrect) versus kappa's 0.659 / 0.903 on the two tasks.

Two attacks in the brief I could NOT sustain, and report against interest. (d) Crashers: measured crash rates were 0.0-9.6%, and the analytic artifact term -n_pass*log(1-c_l) reached only 1.21 nats; corr(crash rate, score) = -0.15. This is a real but second-order bias, not a destroyer of discrimination. (a) Support mismatch: mutant disagreement-support exceeds conceptual-error support by only 1.95x/2.78x, and 23.5% of leap-year mutants landed exactly on the sparse century-year support of the real conceptual error. The "different supports entirely" framing is too strong — this is a calibration problem, not a categorical one. The mechanism dies on the scoring rule, not on the proxy.

The salvageable core is small and is not the proposal: kappa contains ~17.4% cluster-specific variance (R^2 = 0.826 regressing kappa_lj on test-dummy + own-verdict alone), i.e. 83% of it is a restatement of test strictness plus the representative's own pass/fail. At 4.0x the entire baseline execution budget (L*K*M = 2400 vs N*M = 600), that 17% is not purchasable.

findings.claim: The LLR reduces to a monotone-amplified majority vote and therefore cannot rescue candidates on the decisive stratum — the one stratum the method exists to fix.
findings.concrete_demonstration: Exact identity, verified numerically to max|error| = 1.42e-14 in kappa_mech3.py: score_l = SUM_j log(eps_j/kappa_lj) + SUM_{j:PASS}[logit(kappa_lj) + logit(1-eps_j)]. Every passed test contributes a strictly positive amount whenever kappa_lj > eps_j (true in 162/162 cells at eps<=0.10). So the ordering can only re-gain the tally, never invert a verdict. Regressing the KAPPA score on the raw tally across the 9 real clusters: score ~ 3.769*tally - 48.505, R^2 = 0.5935 — the tally that 'never enters the mechanism' explains 59% of it. Ablating ALL cluster-specific variation (kappa_lj -> column mean kappa_.j) yields scores correlated 0.78 with the full mechanism.
findings.fix: Abandon the per-cluster LLR as a selection score. If a specificity term is wanted, it must enter as a per-test weight w_j on a signed contrast between clusters (e.g. weighting DISAGREEMENTS between cluster pairs), not as an additive per-cluster likelihood over a fixed pass row. Any scoring rule whose pass-contribution has fixed positive sign is a reweighted majority vote and must be benchmarked as one.

findings.claim: KAPPA ranks behaviorally IDENTICAL programs differently, by mutant fragility — a syntactic property that is anti-correlated with correctness.
findings.concrete_demonstration: In kappa_real.py the correct program and W_perword produce the identical pass row 111111011111111011 (tally 16 each) — evidentially indistinguishable given that the pass matrix is the only behavioral evidence. KAPPA separates them by 1.42 nats and ranks W_perword (WRONG) above correct. Systematically (kappa_check.py): regressing score on (tally, mean kappa) gives score ~ 3.40*tally + 102.74*mean_kappa - 106.29, R^2 = 0.835 — holding the pass row fixed, +0.10 mean kappa buys +10.27 nats, equivalent to 3.03 free passing tests. And corr(mean kappa, is_correct) = -0.142 across clusters. Net effect: KAPPA picks W_allpos (tally 12), uniform majority picks correct (tally 16); correct places 3rd. Robust to dropping the two deliberately-broken tests (identical result on the 16 clean tests).
findings.fix: Normalize the fragility scale out of kappa before it enters the score — e.g. use the within-cluster centered quantity (kappa_lj - mean_j kappa_lj) so a cluster's overall mutant brittleness cannot buy score. Then re-run: if the centered version has no signal (the R^2=0.826 result suggests ~17% variance remains), the mechanism has nothing left.

findings.claim: eps_j is unobtainable without labels, every available estimator reimports exactly the ACES assumption KAPPA claims to remove — and supplying an ORACLE eps still does not fix the selection.
findings.concrete_demonstration: kappa_mech3.py section (D), four estimators on the real task: pooled candidate pass-rate (= ACES Assumption 4, the pooled reliability KAPPA claims to eliminate) -> picks W_allpos, WRONG. Tally-top cluster as pseudo-correct (= the ACES reference ranking, inverted on the decisive stratum by the proposal's own gap (b)) -> picks W_perword, WRONG. Flat 0.05 -> W_allpos, WRONG. ORACLE eps computed from the true correct program's row, requiring hidden labels -> picks W_perword, still WRONG. Flat-eps sweep over {0.005 ... 0.40}: the argmax is wrong at all nine values, and moves between W_perword and W_allpos at eps=0.05. Clip sweep over {1e-6 ... 0.2} with eps fixed: argmax flips W_allpos -> W_perword at clip=0.01, and the clip bound is unspecified in the design.
findings.fix: State eps_j's estimator before any experiment, and pre-register the clip as a hyperparameter with its tuning protocol. Note that the oracle-eps result means fixing eps will not save the method — this finding should be treated as evidence against the scoring rule, not as a call for a better eps estimator.

findings.claim: kappa at K=20 is too noisy to support the score, because logit(kappa) diverges as kappa->1 and the design's rewards live exactly in that regime.
findings.concrete_demonstration: Delta-method (kappa_check.py): at kappa=0.95, se(kappa)=0.049 and d logit/d kappa = 21.05, giving 1.03 nats of sampling noise PER TEST; at kappa=0.99 it is 2.25 nats/test. A single mutant flipping 19/20 -> 20/20 moves the score by 3.96 nats on that test alone. Over M=18 tests this is ~2.0 nats of pure noise against an observed correct-vs-runner-up margin of 2.39 nats. Bootstrap confirmation (kappa_mech3.py section B): resampling which 20 mutants happen to be generated, over 300 draws, KAPPA selects the correct program only 40.7% of the time (W_perword 30.0%, W_allpos 26.0%). Mutant counts also vary 5-14 across clusters, so the least-sampled clusters get the most extreme kappa estimates and hence the largest bonuses — a selection effect favouring terse programs.
findings.fix: Bound the score contribution by clipping in logit space, not probability space, and report the bootstrap argmax distribution over mutant draws as a required diagnostic. If K must exceed a few hundred to stabilize the argmax, recompute F5: L*K*M already stands at 4.0x the entire baseline execution budget at K=20.

findings.claim: F1 as written cannot falsify the central assumption — a zero-cost, mutant-free null passes it more strongly than kappa does.
findings.concrete_demonstration: kappa_final.py: against true P(fail|incorrect), kappa (costing L*K*M extra executions) achieves corr = +0.659 on count_upper and +0.903 on leap-year. The null 'fraction of CANDIDATES failing test j' — zero mutants, zero extra executions, computable directly from the pass matrix already in hand — achieves +0.998 and +1.000. Both quantities merely track 'is test j discriminating at all'. Separately, corr(kappa, pure test strictness) = +0.888 on leap-year, and regressing kappa_lj on (test dummy + the representative's own verdict) gives R^2 = 0.826, leaving only 17.4% genuinely cluster-specific variance — while the claimed novelty vs ACES is precisely that within-problem cluster variation.
findings.fix: Replace F1 with: (i) corr of the WITHIN-CLUSTER CENTERED residual (kappa_lj - mean_j kappa_lj) against the cluster-LOCAL true P(fail|incorrect), which is the only quantity carrying the claimed novelty; and (ii) a mandatory null-proxy arm — the candidate fail-rate baseline above — that KAPPA must beat. As currently written F1 is passed by a method that generates no mutants at all.

findings.claim: The flagship novelty — negative weight on a test verdict — never fires at plausible eps, and when it fires it is produced by the eps prior rather than by the mutant machinery.
findings.concrete_demonstration: A pass is worth less than a fail iff log((1-eps)/(1-kappa)) < log(eps/kappa), i.e. iff kappa_lj < eps_j. On the real task (kappa_check.py): 0/162 cells at eps=0.01, 0/162 at 0.05, 0/162 at 0.10; the regime only opens at eps=0.20 (6/162, 3.7%) and eps=0.30 (33/162, 20.4%). So the claimed delta over all prior work is gated entirely on eps_j exceeding the local kill rate — i.e. on the assertion that a test false-fails correct code more often than it kills mutants, which is the definition of a broken test — and eps_j is the one parameter the method cannot estimate without labels.
findings.fix: Drop the negative-weight claim as a contribution, or restate it honestly as 'a prior on test brokenness can flip a verdict's sign', which is a property of the eps prior and not of the kappa mechanism. Then show it is not already available to B4 by setting its Beta prior appropriately.

findings.claim: Reported against interest: the crasher objection (d) and the support-mismatch objection (a) do NOT hold at the strength the brief supposes.
findings.concrete_demonstration: Crashers (kappa_mech3.py section C): measured per-cluster mutant crash rates were 0.0-9.6% (median 0.6%). The analytic artifact term -n_pass*log(1-c_l) reached only 1.21 nats (W_reversed) and <=0.10 nats for every other cluster; corr(crash rate, score) = -0.153; the argmax is W_allpos whether crashers are kept or dropped. Crashers do not uniformly saturate kappa. Support mismatch (kappa_support.py): mean disagreement support delta was 0.413 for mutants vs 0.212 for conceptual errors on count_upper (1.95x) and 0.241 vs 0.087 on leap-year (2.78x) — an inflation, not a disjoint support. Notably 23.5% of leap-year mutants landed at delta=0.0032, exactly the sparse century-year support of the real W_no400 conceptual error (e.g. 'y%400 == 0' -> 'y%399 == 0'). AST mutation does reach the thin slice.
findings.fix: Do not build the rebuttal or the defense on these two axes. The 2-3x support inflation is worth correcting via importance-weighting mutants by delta, but it is a calibration fix and will not rescue the scoring rule, which fails independently under oracle kappa and oracle eps.
